content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	  a target-scoped claim instead leases one independent ready target, so
42	  several workers can settle different ready targets of one execution in
43	  parallel;
44	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
45	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
46	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
47	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
48	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
49	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
50	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
51	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
52	  set (delivery is at least once);
53	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
54	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
55	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
56	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
57	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
58	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
59	
60	## Requirements
61	
62	- Python 3.11 or newer
63	- no third-party runtime dependencies
64	
65	## Run the service
66	
67	```bash
68	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
69	```
70	
71	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
72	has bound the port.
73	
74	## HTTP API
75	
76	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
77	
78	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
79	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
80	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
81	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
82	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
83	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
84	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
85	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
86	
87	### Tenants and quotas
88	
89	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
90	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
91	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
92	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
93	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
94	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
95	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
96	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
97	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
98	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
99	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
100	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
101	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
102	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
103	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
104	
105	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
106	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
107	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
108	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
109	history and status queries (the schedule change history included), as well as the quota declaration and delete, the quota
110	read and remaining query, the quota change history, the price
111	declaration and price delete, the price read and the price change history, and the usage, bill, and
112	metrics queries. An empty
113	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
114	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
115	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
116	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
117	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
118	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
119	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
120	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
121	the usual `409 conflict`.
122	
123	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
124	hold:
125	
126	```http
127	PUT /quotas
128	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
129	X-Tenant-Id: acme
130	
131	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
132	```
133	
134	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
135	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer, and may additionally
136	carry the optional `growth` object described below; a non-positive,
137	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
138	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Every quota
139	route requires a tenant: declaring, deleting, and reading without
140	`X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an
141	unknown query parameter on the delete or the remaining query is rejected the
142	same way, with the message naming the offending parameter. The response is
143	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
144	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
145	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
146	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
147	
148	Besides the two limits a declaration may carry one optional `growth` object
149	naming an automatic expansion policy for each limited resource. A policy
150	names only the resources it covers, and a resource it omits is never raised
151	automatically. Each named resource must declare exactly a positive integer
152	`step` and a positive integer `cap`, and the cap must not be below the
153	resource's declared limit:
154	
155	```http
156	PUT /quotas
157	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-2
158	X-Tenant-Id: acme
159	
160	{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}
161	```
162	
163	A missing field, an unknown field (inside the policy or beside it), a
164	non-object policy, a resource other than `workflows` or `executions`, or a
165	step or cap that is non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite is a
166	`400 validation_error`; a cap below the resource's declared limit is rejected
167	the same way. Every such rejection writes nothing. A declaration without
168	`growth` is byte-for-byte the two-limit request above; repeating a declaration
169	replaces limits and policy as a whole, so a declaration that names no `growth`
170	also drops the tenant's previous policy. The declaration response and the
171	quota read include the policy only when one is declared, with each entry
172	listing `step` before `cap` and resources in workflows-first order:
173	
174	```json
175	{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
176	```
177	
178	```http
179	GET /quotas
180	X-Tenant-Id: acme
181	```
182	
183	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
184	when the tenant has declared none.
185	
186	A tenant can also remove the quota it declared, on the same path with the
187	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other quota writes:
188	
189	```http
190	DELETE /quotas
191	Idempotency-Key: quota-delete-1
192	X-Tenant-Id: acme
193	
194	{}
195	```
196	
197	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body, an
198	unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that touches
199	no quota. The delete removes the declaration as a whole and leaves no partial
200	write, so a later read gives the same definite empty result as for a tenant
201	that never declared one: the delete response and every following read both
202	return `{"quota":null}`, and the remaining query lists neither resource —
203	neither limit, holding, nor remaining — and repeats with exactly the same
204	result. Deleting the quota of a tenant that never declared one returns that
205	same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete clears only the
206	declaration: it deletes no existing workflow or execution, and data already
207	held stays fully usable. It writes no metering record, so recorded usage
208	counts and bill conclusions already reached stay exactly as they were; later
209	writes simply run without a quota check until the tenant declares again.
210	
211	The delete follows the same idempotency rules as every other write: the
212	`Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same delete with the same
213	key returns the first result and performs no second removal, and reusing a
214	key for another operation — including a quota declaration — in the same
215	tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's quota unchanged. Quotas
216	are scoped per tenant like everything else: deleting one tenant's quota never
217	affects another tenant's declaration or remaining room. A missing or empty
218	tenant and a missing idempotency key are `400 validation_error`, and every
219	failed validation writes nothing — no quota row, no metering record, and no
220	quota or price-table change history.
221	
222	A separate read-only entry point reports how much room the declared quota
223	leaves, with the same calling shape as the quota read:
224	
225	```http
226	GET /quotas/status
227	X-Tenant-Id: acme
228	```
229	
230	Each limited resource gives three numbers — the declared `limit`, the
231	`held` count the quota decision itself uses, and the `remaining` room, which
232	is simply limit minus holding — in that key order, with workflows first and
233	executions second; the same query repeats with the same ordering:
234	
235	```json
236	{"status":{"workflows":{"limit":10,"held":3,"remaining":7},"executions":{"limit":100,"held":12,"remaining":88}}}
237	```
238	
239	Lowering a limit below the current holding reports the `remaining` room
240	truthfully as a negative number; it is neither clamped to zero nor rejected.
241	A tenant that has never declared a quota gets the definite empty result
242	`{"status":null}`, listing neither resource. The query is strictly read-only:
243	it writes no metering record and changes no declared quota, usage, bill,
244	scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion, and another tenant's quota and
245	holdings are never visible and never influence the result. It requires a
246	tenant and accepts no query parameters: a missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id`
247	header, an unknown parameter (named in the error message), or a repeated
248	parameter is a `400 validation_error`, and these rejections write nothing.
249	
250	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the write is admitted
251	once the resource declares a growth policy that can make room: the declared
252	limit is raised in whole steps — the smallest number of `step` increments
253	that admits the write — never past the `cap` and never by a partial final
254	step, and the raised limit commits with the write in the same transaction,
255	so the request succeeds instead of returning a conflict. The expansion
256	changes only the declared limit: it writes no metering record, changes no
257	recorded usage count, and changes no bill conclusion already reached.
258	Repeating the same write with the same idempotency key returns the first
259	result without a second expansion, and reusing that key for another
260	operation is the usual `409 conflict`. Without a policy on the resource, or
261	when no whole-step raise within the cap can admit the write — including when
262	the cap already leaves no room for one more holding — the whole request is
263	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
264	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
265	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
266	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write and leaves the limit
267	untouched: nothing is inserted and previously stored data is unaffected,
268	exactly as for validation failures. The quota read and the remaining query
269	report the raised limit; the remaining query's `remaining` room is computed
270	from it.
271	
272	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
273	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
274	is at its execution limit, a growth policy raises the limit exactly as for a
275	manual creation and the period fires normally; when there is no policy or
276	the cap leaves no room a whole step can reach, the due period creates no
277	execution and the schedule is left unchanged — its cursor,
278	`last_triggered_at`, and `last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the
279	period is settled on a later pass once capacity exists, under the usual
280	per-period idempotence. Delivery history follows the tenant of the execution
281	it belongs to.
282	
283	### Quota change history
284	
285	Every successful quota declaration or delete leaves one change record, so a
286	caller can see exactly when each quota declaration and each removal took
287	effect. A separate read-only entry point returns the tenant's change history
288	with the same calling shape as the price-table change history:
289	
290	```http
291	GET /quotas/history?limit=50
292	X-Tenant-Id: acme
293	```
294	
295	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
296	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
297	Each record is:
298	
299	```json
300	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
301	```
302	
303	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
304	  shared across both kinds of quota change. It identifies the record across
305	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
306	- `action` is `declare` for a quota declaration or `delete` for a removal;
307	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
308	  ending in `Z`;
309	- `snapshot` is the complete quota in effect after the change. A
310	  declaration's snapshot is the limits and growth policy that took effect:
311	  the two limits first, `workflows` before `executions`, followed by the
312	  optional `growth` object containing only the resources this declaration
313	  named, each entry listing `step` before `cap`; a declaration without a
314	  growth policy lists no `growth` at all. A delete's snapshot is `null`.
315	
316	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
317	same transaction as the quota write, so a reader always sees the declaration
318	and its history agree and a declaration or delete rejected by validation, a
319	quota conflict, or an idempotency-key conflict leaves no record. Repeating an
320	idempotent declaration or delete with the same key returns the first result
321	and appends no second record; reusing a key for another operation is the
322	usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no history. Deleting the quota of a
323	tenant that never declared one still succeeds and still leaves its own
324	`delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns the definite
325	empty result for the quota itself.
326	
327	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
328	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
329	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
330	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
331	
332	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
333	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination, in exactly
334	the same shape as the price-table change history:
335	
336	```http
337	GET /quotas/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
338	```
339	
340	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
341	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
342	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
343	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
344	  returned;
345	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
346	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
347	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
348	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
349	  and the definite empty list is returned;
350	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
351	  contains more than that many records;
352	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
353	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
354	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
355	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
356	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
357	
358	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
359	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
360	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
361	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
362	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records, and another tenant's history
363	is never visible under any filter. The query is read-only: it appends no
364	history, writes no metering record, and changes no quota declaration, usage,
365	bill, scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion. A quota declaration or
366	delete not participating in this change — reads, the remaining query,
367	scheduling, metering, and billing included — is byte-for-byte unchanged, and
368	no metering record is added. After a replay or a recovery each record's
369	sequence, occurrence time, and snapshot stay exactly as they were first
370	written.
371	
372	### Tenant price tables
373	
374	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
375	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
376	the quota declaration:
377	
378	```http
379	PUT /prices
380	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
381	X-Tenant-Id: acme
382	
383	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
384	```
385	
386	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
387	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
388	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
389	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
390	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
391	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
392	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
393	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
394	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
395	offending parameter. The response is
396	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
397	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
398	
399	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
400	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
401	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
402	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
403	before it was made.
404	
405	```http
406	GET /prices
407	X-Tenant-Id: acme
408	```
409	
410	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
411	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
412	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
413	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
414	
415	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
416	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
417	
418	```http
419	DELETE /prices
420	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
421	X-Tenant-Id: acme
422	
423	{}
424	```
425	
426	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
427	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
428	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
429	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
430	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
431	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
432	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
433	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
434	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
435	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
436	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
437	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
438	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
439	
440	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
441	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
442	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
443	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
444	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
445	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
446	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
447	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
448	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
449	
450	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
451	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
452	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
453	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
454	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
455	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
456	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
457	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
458	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
459	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
460	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
461	as they were.
462	
463	### Price-table change history
464	
465	Every successful price-table declaration or delete leaves one change record,
466	so a caller can see exactly when each repricing and each table removal took
467	effect. A separate entry point returns the tenant's change history:
468	
469	```http
470	GET /prices/history?limit=50
471	X-Tenant-Id: acme
472	```
473	
474	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
475	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
476	Each record is:
477	
478	```json
479	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"execution_started":200}}
480	```
481	
482	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
483	  shared across every kind of price change. It identifies the record across
484	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
485	- `action` is `declare` for a price-table declaration or `delete` for a
486	  removal;
487	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
488	  ending in `Z`;
489	- `snapshot` is the table in effect after the change. A declaration's
490	  snapshot is the type-to-unit-price map that took effect, listing only the
491	  types that declaration named and in ascending type-identifier order; a
492	  delete's snapshot is `null`.
493	
494	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
495	same transaction as the price-table write, so a reader always sees the table
496	and its history agree and a rejected declaration, delete, or idempotency-key
497	conflict leaves no record. Repeating an idempotent declaration or delete with
498	the same key returns the first result and appends no second record; reusing a
499	key for another operation is the usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no
500	history. A delete of a table that was never declared still succeeds and still
501	leaves its own `delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns
502	the definite empty result for the table itself.
503	
504	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
505	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
506	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
507	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
508	
509	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
510	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination:
511	
512	```http
513	GET /prices/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
514	```
515	
516	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
517	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
518	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
519	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
520	  returned;
521	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
522	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
523	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
524	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
525	  and the definite empty list is returned;
526	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
527	  contains more than that many records;
528	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
529	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
530	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
531	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
532	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
533	
534	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
535	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
536	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
537	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
538	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
539	appends no history, changes no price table, and changes no metering, usage,
540	bill, quota, or scheduling conclusion. History follows the usual tenant
541	isolation, so another tenant's changes are never visible under any action
542	filter, window, or page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and
543	recovery leave every recorded sequence, time, and snapshot unchanged.
544	
545	### Usage metering and billing
546	
547	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
548	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
549	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
550	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
551	metered action types are:
552	
553	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
554	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
555	  definition;
556	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
557	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
558	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
559	  `schedule_triggered`;
560	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
561	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
562	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
563	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
564	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
565	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
566	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
567	  meters nothing.
568	
569	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
570	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
571	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
572	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
573	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
574	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
575	
576	```http
577	GET /usage
578	X-Tenant-Id: acme
579	```
580	
581	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
582	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
583	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
584	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
585	
586	```http
587	GET /bill
588	X-Tenant-Id: acme
589	```
590	
591	Returns the per-type bill:
592	
593	```json
594	{"bill":{"items":[
595	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
596	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
597	],"total":2100}}
598	```
599	
600	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
601	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
602	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
603	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
604	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
605	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
606	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
607	billed byte for byte as before.
608	
609	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
610	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
611	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
612	bucket:
613	
614	```http
615	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
616	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
617	X-Tenant-Id: acme
618	```
619	
620	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
621	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
622	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
623	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
624	  as before;
625	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
626	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
627	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
628	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
629	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
630	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
631	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
632	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
633	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
634	  `0`.
635	
636	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
637	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
638	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
639	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
640	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
641	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
642	
643	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
644	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
645	themselves:
646	
647	```http
648	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
649	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
650	X-Tenant-Id: acme
651	```
652	
653	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
654	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
655	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
656	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
657	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
658	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
659	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
660	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
661	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
662	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
663	  record in the bucket is omitted;
664	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
665	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
666	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
667	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
668	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
669	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
670	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
671	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
672	  integer cents;
673	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
674	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
675	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
676	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
677	  total at `0`;
678	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
679	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
680	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
681	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
682	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
683	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
684	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
685	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
686	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
687	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
688	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
689	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
690	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
691	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
692	
693	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
694	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
695	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
696	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
697	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
698	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
699	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
700	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
701	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
702	
703	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
704	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
705	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
706	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
707	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
708	
709	### Per-record usage history
710	
711	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
712	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
713	checked against the moment it occurred:
714	
715	```http
716	GET /usage/records?limit=50
717	X-Tenant-Id: acme
718	```
719	
720	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
721	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
722	sequence. Each record is:
723	
724	```json
725	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
726	```
727	
728	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
729	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
730	  filter or a page;
731	- `type` is the metered action type;
732	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
733	  ending in `Z`.
734	
735	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
736	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
737	like every other JSON endpoint.
738	
739	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
740	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
741	pagination:
742	
743	```http
744	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
745	```
746	
747	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
748	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
749	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
750	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
751	  returned, exactly as before;
752	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
753	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
754	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
755	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
756	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
757	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
758	  contains more than that many records;
759	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
760	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
761	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
762	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
763	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
764	
765	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
766	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
767	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
768	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
769	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
770	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
771	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
772	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
773	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
774	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.

776	### Operational metrics
777	
778	```http
779	GET /metrics
780	X-Tenant-Id: acme
781	```
782	
783	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
784	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
785	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
786	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
787	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
788	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
789	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
790	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
791	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
792	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
793	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
794	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
795	
796	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
797	timestamp ending in `Z`:
798	
799	```http
800	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
801	X-Tenant-Id: acme
802	```
803	
804	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
805	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
806	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
807	  counts every recorded fact;
808	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
809	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
810	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
811	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
812	  result.
813	
814	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
815	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
816	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
817	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
818	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
819	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
820	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
821	completion or termination event.
822	
823	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
824	
825	```http
826	GET /metrics/export
827	X-Tenant-Id: acme
828	```
829	
830	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
831	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
832	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
833	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
834	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
835	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
836	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
837	
838	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
839	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
840	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
841	ordered by ascending label value:
842	
843	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
844	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
845	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
846	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
847	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
848	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
849	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
850	  unlabeled scalar samples.
851	
852	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
853	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
854	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
855	ends with a single newline.
856	
857	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
858	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
859	failures, and schedule triggers:
860	
861	```json
862	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
863	```
864	
865	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
866	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
867	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
868	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
869	  ended for that reason.
870	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
871	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
872	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
873	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
874	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
875	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
876	  another attempt, per node identifier.
877	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
878	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
879	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
880	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
881	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
882	
883	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
884	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
885	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
886	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
887	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
888	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
889	
890	### Health
891	
892	```http
893	GET /health
894	```
895	
896	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
897	
898	### Create a workflow
899	
900	```http
901	POST /workflows
902	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
903	
904	{
905	  "id": "order-flow",
906	  "nodes": [
907	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
908	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
909	  ]
910	}
911	```
912	
913	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
914	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
915	
916	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
917	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
918	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
919	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
920	
921	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
922	
923	```json
924	{
925	  "id": "order-flow",
926	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
927	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
928	}
929	```
930	
931	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
932	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
933	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
934	
935	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
936	
937	```json
938	{
939	  "id": "nightly-orders",
940	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
941	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
942	}
943	```
944	
945	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
946	
947	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
948	
949	```json
950	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
951	```
952	
953	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
954	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
955	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
956	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
957	`false`.
958	
959	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
960	
961	```json
962	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
963	```
964	
965	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
966	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
967	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
968	dependencies of its successors.
969	
970	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
971	
972	```json
973	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
974	```
975	
976	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
977	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
978	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
979	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
980	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
981	`retries_exhausted`.
982	
983	A task may instead declare an approval point:
984	
985	```json
986	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
987	```
988	
989	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
990	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
991	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
992	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
993	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
994	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
995	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
996	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
997	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
998	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
999	move the task.
1000	
1001	### Submit an approval decision
1002	
1003	```http
1004	POST /executions/run-1/decision
1005	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
1006	
1007	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
1008	```
1009	
1010	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
1011	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
1012	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
1013	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
1014	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
1015	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
1016	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
1017	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
1018	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
1019	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
1020	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
1021	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
1022	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
1023	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
1024	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
1025	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
1026	404.
1027	
1028	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
1029	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
1030	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
1031	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
1032	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
1033	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
1034	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
1035	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
1036	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
1037	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
1038	shape and event stream.
1039	
1040	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
1041	segment:
1042	
1043	```json
1044	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
1045	```
1046	
1047	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
1048	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
1049	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
1050	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
1051	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
1052	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
1053	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
1054	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
1055	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
1056	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
1057	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
1058	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
1059	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
1060	loop node instead).
1061	
1062	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
1063	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
1064	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
1065	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
1066	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
1067	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
1068	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
1069	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
1070	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
1071	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
1072	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
1073	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
1074	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
1075	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
1076	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
1077	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
1078	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
1079	belong only to their iterations.
1080	
1081	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
1082	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
1083	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
1084	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
1085	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
1086	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
1087	exactly.
1088	
1089	### Dynamic map nodes
1090	
1091	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
1092	recorded array:
1093	
1094	```json
1095	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
1096	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
1097	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
1098	```
1099	
1100	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
1101	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
1102	
1103	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
1104	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
1105	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
1106	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
1107	  the same path syntax as a condition.
1108	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
1109	  expand.
1110	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
1111	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
1112	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
1113	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
1114	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
1115	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
1116	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
1117	
1118	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
1119	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
1120	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
1121	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
1122	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
1123	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
1124	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
1125	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
1126	overwrite another instance.
1127	
1128	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
1129	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
1130	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
1131	become available in the usual way.
1132	
1133	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
1134	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
1135	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
1136	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
1137	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
1138	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1139	
1140	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
1141	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
1142	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
1143	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
1144	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
1145	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
1146	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
1147	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
1148	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
1149	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
1150	
1151	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
1152	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
1153	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
1154	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
1155	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
1156	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
1157	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
1158	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
1159	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
1160	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
1161	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
1162	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
1163	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
1164	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
1165	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
1166	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
1167	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
1168	
1169	### Maps inside loop bodies
1170	
1171	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
1172	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
1173	other body member:
1174	
1175	```json
1176	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
1177	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
1178	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
1179	```
1180	
1181	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
1182	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
1183	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
1184	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
1185	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
1186	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
1187	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
1188	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
1189	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1190	
1191	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
1192	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
1193	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
1194	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
1195	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
1196	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
1197	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
1198	influence from the iteration number.
1199	
1200	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
1201	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
1202	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
1203	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
1204	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
1205	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
1206	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
1207	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
1208	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
1209	
1210	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
1211	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
1212	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
1213	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
1214	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
1215	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
1216	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
1217	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
1218	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
1219	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
1220	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
1221	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
1222	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
1223	
1224	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
1225	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
1226	
1227	### Delete and modify expanded instances
1228	
1229	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
1230	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
1231	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
1232	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
1233	
1234	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
1235	that has permanently failed:
1236	
1237	```http
1238	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
1239	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
1240	
1241	{}
1242	```
1243	
1244	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
1245	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
1246	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
1247	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
1248	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
1249	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
1250	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
1251	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
1252	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
1253	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
1254	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
1255	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
1256	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
1257	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
1258	
1259	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
1260	before it is worked:
1261	
1262	```http
1263	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
1264	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
1265	
1266	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
1267	```
1268	
1269	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
1270	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
1271	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
1272	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
1273	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
1274	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
1275	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
1276	is stored verbatim.
1277	
1278	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
1279	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
1280	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
1281	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
1282	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
1283	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
1284	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
1285	
1286	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
1287	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
1288	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
1289	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1290	carries no loop context.
1291	
1292	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1293	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1294	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1295	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1296	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1297	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1298	first result and appends no second event.
1299	
1300	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1301	
1302	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1303	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1304	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1305	  and `iteration`;
1306	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1307	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1308	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1309	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1310	
1311	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1312	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1313	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1314	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1315	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1316	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1317	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1318	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1319	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1320	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1321	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1322	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1323	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1324	
1325	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1326	
1327	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1328	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1329	
1330	```http
1331	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1332	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1333	
1334	{}
1335	```
1336	
1337	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1338	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1339	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1340	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1341	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1342	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1343	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1344	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1345	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1346	bounds start from zero.
1347	
1348	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1349	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1350	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1351	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1352	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1353	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1354	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1355	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1356	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1357	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1358	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1359	expansion.
1360	
1361	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1362	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1363	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1364	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1365	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1366	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1367	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1368	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1369	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1370	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1371	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1372	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1373	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1374	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1375	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1376	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1377	an instance that stayed deleted.
1378	
1379	### Workflow versions
1380	
1381	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1382	
1383	```json
1384	{
1385	  "id": "order-flow",
1386	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1387	  "nodes": [
1388	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1389	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1390	  ]
1391	}
1392	```
1393	
1394	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
